/-!
# Bugeaud Collection of Conjectures and Open Questions: Confined Powers of Non-Pisot Numbers

*References:*
  - [Bug12a] Bugeaud, Yann. "Distribution modulo one and Diophantine approximation."
    Vol. 193. Cambridge University Press, 2012. Chapter 10.
  - [Bug12b] Bugeaud, Yann, and Nikolay Moshchevitin. "On fractional parts of powers
    of real numbers close to 1." Mathematische Zeitschrift 271.3 (2012): 627-637.
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Bugeaud07

/--
Problem 10.7. Let $\varepsilon$ be a positive real number. Are there arbitrarily
large real numbers $\alpha$ such that $\alpha$ is not a Pisot number and all the
fractional parts $\{\alpha^n\}$, $n \ge 1$, are lying in an interval of length
$\varepsilon / \alpha$? [Bug12b]
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem problem_10_7 : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → ∀ M : ℝ, ∃ α : ℝ, M < α ∧ ¬ IsPisot α ∧
      ∃ c : ℝ, ∀ n : ℕ, 1 ≤ n → Int.fract (α ^ n) ∈ Set.Icc c (c + ε / α) := by
  sorry

end Bugeaud07

reformulations.difference: The source says the fractional parts lie in 'an interval of length ε/α'. The Lean uses a closed interval `Set.Icc c (c + ε / α)` with c ∈ ℝ, and writes 'arbitrarily large α' as `∀ M, ∃ α, M < α`.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For a fixed ε, lying in a closed interval of length L is weaker than lying in an open one of length L. But the right-hand side quantifies over every ε > 0. A closed interval [c, c+ε/(2α)] sits inside the open interval (c − ε/(4α), c + 3ε/(4α)), which has length ε/α (α > 0 because α > max M 0). The converse direction is Ioo ⊆ Icc. So the ∀ε statement is the same for closed and open intervals, and it cannot depend on the interval type the source leaves unspecified. Likewise `∀ M, ∃ α > M, P α` is equivalent to the set {α | P α} not being bounded above. Both equivalences were proved in a Lean scratch file against the file's exact right-hand side.

could_not_verify: Bugeaud07.problem_10_7: I could not read the book's own wording of Problem 10.7 [Bug12a, Ch. 10]. Cambridge Core only previews Problems 10.1–10.3, and Google Books was blocked. So I also could not confirm that the problem is numbered 10.7 there. I checked faithfulness against the paper [Bug12b], which the docstring cites and quotes word for word; that is where the question was first posed.
review.notes:
No defects found. Points checked:
(1) Scope of ε. The source says 'Let ε be a positive real number. Are there …?'. The Lean puts ∀ ε > 0 inside the `answer(sorry)` equivalence, which is the standard reading and the repository's convention (compare Erdős 137, 'Let k ≥ 3. Can …'). The property is monotone in ε. It already holds for every ε > 2: Vijayaraghavan's Theorem V2 in the paper gives α ∈ (H, H+1) with all {α^n} in any prescribed interval of length > 2/H. Choosing that interval away from 0 and 1 forces α to be non-Pisot. So the open content is exactly the small-ε case, and '∀ ε > 0' captures it. Also, α is chosen after ε and c after α, as in the source.
(2) `IsPisot` matches the paper's definition: algebraic integer > 1 whose other conjugates lie in the open unit disc. I proved in Lean that `IsPisot (k : ℝ)` holds for every natural k ≥ 2, and that without the `¬ IsPisot α` conjunct the right-hand side is trivially true (integers k ≥ 2 give {k^n} = 0). So the non-Pisot condition does real work and correctly excludes the degenerate witnesses. `answer(sorry)` has type Prop and the right-hand side is not negated.
(3) 'Interval' is read as a real interval containing the fractional parts in [0,1), not as an arc mod 1. That is the literal reading and matches how the paper uses intervals in Theorem V2 and Theorem 3.
(4) Status. I found no resolution of the question. The works citing Bugeaud–Moshchevitin (Baker 2014, Schleischitz 2015, Bugeaud–Liao–Rams 2017, Moshchevitin's 2012 survey, and others) do not address it. Known Pisot-forcing results work at the scale ~1/(α² log α) for ‖α^n‖, and known constructions give length ~2/α, so the question is still open. `research open` is consistent with this. The search could not cover journal-only papers exhaustively (e.g. by Dubickas).
